body.text: Nine verbs that follow none of the usual rules

Nine verbs in English add an attitude to another verb. They are *can*, *could*, *may*, *might*, *will*, *would*, *shall*, *should* and *must*. Each one says how sure you are, how necessary something is, or what you are allowed to do.

body.lead_in: A modal verb behaves in five ways that no ordinary verb does:
items: the verb after it is the base form, with no *to*
it never takes *-s*, whoever the subject is
it has no *-ing* form and no third form of its own
it makes its own questions and negatives, with no *do*
two modals never stand together in one verb group

body.caption: One shape for every person. No *-s*, no *do*, no *to* after it.
body.form_line: a modal + the base form of the verb, with no *to*

rows.note: The full negative is written as one word: *cannot*.
*May I…?* asks permission. *May she…?* is rare.
*mightn't* is British and rare. *might not* is safe everywhere.
In everyday English *shall* survives mainly in offers and suggestions.

body.text: The gaps the nine modals leave, and what fills them

A modal has one shape and no others. So there is no past *must*, no future *can*, and no way to put a modal after another modal. English fills every one of those gaps with a helper made of two or three words.

body.gloss: a helper made of more than one word: *have to*, *be able to*

show_first.text: Drivers have to renew the permit every spring.
The clinic was able to see everybody before six.
You had better keep the receipt.

body.name_line: A helper like that is called a **semi-modal**.
body.anchor_line: It means what a modal means, and it changes shape like an ordinary verb. That is the point of it.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: You had better to book the coach seat early.
body.right: You had better book the coach seat early.
body.why_it_happens: *Have to*, *need to* and *ought to* all end in *to*, so *to* starts to look like part of every helper. *Had better* is one of the four that take the base form on its own.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the *to*. Four helpers take no *to*: *had better*, *would rather*, *be going to*, *be about to*.

body.wrong: The panel ought publish the raw figures as well.
body.right: The panel ought to publish the raw figures as well.
body.why_it_happens: *Ought* means what *should* means, and *should* takes no *to*, so the *to* gets dropped along with the meaning it came with.
body.smallest_fix: Keep *ought* and *to* together. They are one helper and they never separate.

body.wrong: I am used to live in Sandmouth, but I moved away in 2019.
body.right: I used to live in Sandmouth, but I moved away in 2019.
body.why_it_happens: *Used to* and *be used to* are spelled the same, so one gets reached for when the other is meant. Adding *am* switches the sentence from a finished past to a present feeling.
body.smallest_fix: For a finished past, drop the *be*: *I used to live*. Keep *be used to* for what feels normal now.

body.label: Three oddities in this set, one of them worth learning today

items.text: In the negative and the question, *used* loses its *-d*, because *did* already carries the past.
items.example: Did you use to cycle in, or did you always drive?

items.text: *Didn't used to* is written and said by many people, and plenty of reference books now list it. *Didn't use to* is the safer form to write.
items.example: The library didn't use to open on Sundays.

items.text: *Need* and *dare* work as ordinary verbs and, in questions and negatives only, as modals. The modal versions are formal and mainly British.
items.example: You needn't send the second reference.

article_json.also_called: Modality of certainty: deduction and possibility in the present
article_json.one_line: This lets you say how sure you are about something, instead of stating everything as a flat fact.
article_json.short_answer: Sure it is true, use *must*. Sure it is not, use *can't*. Anything in between, use *may*, *might* or *could*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say I think something is true without saying it is?

body.text: Every modal here answers one question: how sure are you?

*The lights are on in the office* is a fact you can see. *Somebody must be working late* is not a fact. It is what you work out from the fact, and the modal is what tells your reader you worked it out.
So the choice is not really between words. It is a choice about how far you are prepared to go on the evidence you have.

body.caption: One line from certain-yes to certain-no, with the middle left open.

steps.gloss: I am confident this is true
I expect it to be true

steps.text: may be, might be, could be
may not be, might not be

steps.gloss: I am confident this is not true

body.text: How to build it, and where the negative goes

body.caption: *Can't* is the opposite of *must*. *May not* is the opposite of nothing.
rows: you expect it not to be so
footnotes: *Could not be* does not mean *possibly not*. It means the same as *can't be*.

body.lead_in: One situation, five degrees of confidence. Only the modal changes.

items.text: The lift is out again, so the engineer must be on site.
items.gloss: You are confident the engineer is there.

items.text: The engineer should be on site by now.
items.gloss: You expect him to be there, from the usual timings.

items.text: The engineer may be on site already.
items.gloss: It is possible that he is there.

items.text: The engineer might not be on site until Thursday.
items.gloss: Possibly he will not be there before Thursday.

items.text: The van has gone, so the engineer can't be on site.
items.gloss: You are confident he is not there.

body.so_what: Nothing about the office changed across those five sentences. What changed is how much the speaker is willing to claim.

body.text: Use *must* when you are confident something is true, *can't* when you are confident it is not, and *may*, *might* or *could* in between.

body.lead_in: Each of these draws a conclusion from something visible in the sentence before it.

items.text: Her coat is still here, so she must be in the building.
items.gloss: The coat is the evidence. You are confident she is inside.

items.text: The figures could be out of date, so check the source first.
items.gloss: Old figures are one real possibility here.

items.text: That can't be the final total, because it is smaller than the first quarter.
items.gloss: The number is impossible, so it is not the final one.

items.text: The rise may reflect a change in how the data is collected.
items.gloss: A change in method is one possible reason for the rise.

body.so_what: Each sentence names its evidence and then says how far that evidence goes. That is the whole job of the modal.

body.text: So which of *may*, *might* and *could* do I write?

body.question: How formal am I being, and am I offering one option among several?

options.label: *may*
options.use_it_when: You are writing, and you want a careful, formal way of saying that something is possible.
options.example: The shortfall may be the result of a slower spring.

options.label: *might*
options.use_it_when: You are speaking or writing, and you want the everyday word for a possibility.
options.example: The shortfall might be the result of a slower spring.

options.label: *could*
options.use_it_when: You are naming one possibility out of two or three that you can see.
options.example: The shortfall could be a slower spring, or simply a counting error.

a.text: The delay may be weather-related.
a.means: Bad weather is a real possible cause, and you are being careful about saying so.

b.text: The delay can be weather-related.
b.means: Delays of this kind are sometimes caused by weather. You are describing what happens in general.

a.text: The results might not arrive before Friday.
a.means: Possibly they will not come by Friday.

b.text: The results couldn't arrive before Friday.
b.means: Friday is impossible. There is no way of getting them sooner.

a.text: You may leave your bag at the desk.
a.means: You are allowed to leave it there.

b.text: You may lose your bag at the desk.
b.means: Losing it there is possible, so be careful.

a.text: The council could fund the repair.
a.means: Funding it is one option open to them.

b.text: The council should fund the repair.
b.means: You expect them to, or you think they ought to.

body.deciding_factor: *May* is the formal one, *might* the everyday one, and *could* the one that offers an option. All three mean it is possible.
body.trap: You were told *might* is less likely than *may*, so you spend time weighing the two when the real difference is how formal the sentence is.
body.register_note: *May* is the safer choice in Task 1 and Task 2 when you explain a cause. *Might* and *could* are natural in Speaking Part 3 speculation.

body.text: *May* and *might* are very close in meaning, and speakers do not agree about which is weaker. What is reliable is that *may* is the more formal of the two, and that *might* is the form you use when you report what somebody said.
The word *may* is doing two different jobs

body.lead_in: The same word twice, once about possibility and once about permission.

items.text: The scheme may run for a second year.
items.gloss: A second year is possible. Nobody has decided.

items.text: Students may use the west entrance after six.
items.gloss: They are allowed to use it after six.

items.text: The hall may be booked for private events.
items.gloss: Booking it privately is permitted — or possible. The sentence alone does not say which.

items.text: May I take one of these leaflets?
items.gloss: You are asking for permission.

body.so_what: In a question, *may* always asks permission. In a statement, the sentence around it tells you which job it is doing.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The windows are dark, so the family mustn't be at home.
body.right: The windows are dark, so the family can't be at home.
body.why_it_happens: *Must* is the confident word, so its negative looks like the confident negative. *Mustn't* was never about certainty at all — it forbids something.
body.smallest_fix: Swap *mustn't* for *can't*. The opposite of *must be* is *can't be*.

body.wrong: I have not seen the report, so the fall must be caused by the new charge.
body.right: I have not seen the report, so the fall may be caused by the new charge.
body.why_it_happens: *Must* feels like a strong, academic word, so it gets used to sound confident. It claims that you are sure, and the first half of the sentence has just said you are not.
body.smallest_fix: Use *may* or *might* whenever you have not seen the evidence yourself.

body.wrong: She is not answering her phone, so she can be in the meeting.
body.right: She is not answering her phone, so she may be in the meeting.
body.why_it_happens: *Can* does mean possible, but only about what happens in general — *evenings here can be cold*. For one occasion happening now, English uses *may*, *might* or *could*.
body.smallest_fix: For a guess about this moment, write *may*, *might* or *could*, never *can*.

body.heard: *Might* means it is less likely than *may*.
also_known_as: *may* is 50 per cent and *might* is 30 per cent
body.truth: Many speakers do feel *might* as slightly more remote, but they do not agree with each other, and no reader can tell the two apart in your writing. The reliable difference is that *may* is the more formal word.
body.what_to_do: Stop weighing them. Write *may* in an essay, say *might* in speech, and put the real strength in the words around the modal if it matters.

body.mechanism: Russian carries this meaning with small separate words placed near the verb, such as the words for *probably* and *perhaps*.
body.wrong: Probably the engineer is on site now.
body.right: The engineer may be on site now.
body.fix: Put the doubt in the verb group with a modal. English prefers that to an added word.

body.text: Working out what happened, when you were not there

You come back to the site and the trench is full of water. You did not see it fill. *The pump must have failed overnight* says what you have worked out, and it says openly that you are working it out.
Learners usually avoid this whole structure and write *maybe the pump failed* instead. That is understandable English, and it throws away the difference between what you saw and what you concluded.
How to build it: modal, then *have*, then the third form

examples.text: The road was already clear, so the tide must have turned early.
examples.gloss: You are confident the tide turned before you arrived.

examples.text: They can't have finished the survey; the equipment is still out there.
examples.gloss: You are confident the survey is not done.

examples.text: The drop may have begun before the new charge was introduced.
examples.gloss: It is possible the fall started earlier than people assume.

examples.text: The file might not have reached the second reviewer at all.
examples.gloss: Possibly the second reviewer never got it.

examples.text: They could've taken the coast road instead.
examples.gloss: The coast road was an option they had.

notes: *must've* and *might've* are what you hear. They sound like *must of*, and *must of* is never written.
The word after *have* is the third form: *written*, *taken*, *begun*, never the past form.
There is no *to* anywhere in this structure.

body.caption: The event is back there. The guessing is happening now.

body.text: To guess about the past, keep the modal you would use about now, and put *have* plus the third form behind it.

body.lead_in: The same guess about now, then about earlier. Only the second half of the verb group moves.

items.text: The heating must be broken.
items.gloss: You are confident it is broken at this moment.

items.text: The heating must have broken during the night.
items.gloss: You are confident it broke while nobody was there.

items.text: The panel may be using last year's figures.
items.gloss: Possibly they are working from old figures right now.

items.text: The panel may have used last year's figures.
items.gloss: Possibly the figures they worked from were the old ones.

body.so_what: The modal did not change in either pair. *Have* plus the third form is what moved the guess into the past.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The subsidy must contributed to the rise in applications.
body.right: The subsidy must have contributed to the rise in applications.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past form of the verb goes in and feels like enough. The modal cannot carry past time by itself, and *have* is the part that does it.
body.smallest_fix: Put *have* in, and change the verb to the third form: *must have contributed*.

body.wrong: She might have wrote to the department in March.
body.right: She might have written to the department in March.
body.why_it_happens: For most verbs the past form and the third form are the same word, so the difference never comes up. It comes up on the irregular verbs, and those are the commonest ones.
body.smallest_fix: After *have*, use the third form: *written*, *taken*, *done*, *seen*.

body.wrong: The gate was locked, so the delivery mustn't have arrived.
body.right: The gate was locked, so the delivery can't have arrived.
body.why_it_happens: You want the negative of *must have*, and *mustn't have* looks like it. *Mustn't* forbids things and cannot make a guess at all.
body.smallest_fix: Write *can't have* or *couldn't have* for a confident negative guess about the past.

body.label: Three cases that behave differently, one of them a real meaning difference

items.text: *Needn't have* + third form says the thing was done and was unnecessary. *Didn't need to* says only that it was not necessary.
items.example: You needn't have queued — the tickets were emailed that morning.

items.text: American English also uses *must not have* for a confident negative guess. British English uses *can't have* there. Both are correct at home.
items.example: He must not have seen the second notice.

items.text: *Could have* + third form has a second meaning: it was possible and it did not happen.
items.example: The council could have funded the repair, but the money went elsewhere.

body.stop_line: That is the whole list. Anything else that looks like a fourth case is one of these three wearing different words.

body.heard: *Must have gone* is the past tense of *must go*.

body.text: The difference is a strong tendency, not a border. Speakers cross it often, and *have to* is slowly taking over in speech. Where the two really part company is the past, and there the choice is made for you.

body.text: The same six words, and two opposite instructions
*You mustn't tell them* and *you don't have to tell them* look like two versions of one sentence. One of them forbids you from telling. The other says telling is up to you.

articles.title: *Should*, *ought to*, and the one that is a warning

article_json.also_called: Advice and expectation: *should*, *ought to*, *had better*, *be supposed to*
article_json.one_line: This lets you recommend something without ordering it, and shows you which word turns advice into a warning.

body.text: Advice sits between an order and a suggestion
*Keep a copy* is an instruction. *You could keep a copy* is one option among several. *You should keep a copy* sits between them: you are recommending it, and the other person still decides.
Three other helpers live in the same area, and one of them is not advice at all. Getting that one wrong changes a friendly sentence into a threat.
How to build the four, including the negatives

body.caption: Two take *to*. *Had better* takes none, and its *not* comes last.
footnotes: *Had better* is nearly always shortened in speech to *'d better*.
*Ought not to* is rare. Most people write *shouldn't*.

body.text: Two different things, and English uses one word for both
*She can drive* says she has the skill. *You can park here* says nobody will stop you. English uses *can* for both, and the sentence around it tells you which one is meant.
The hard part is not the present. It is the past, because English splits past ability into two forms and most learners are given only one of them.

body.deciding_factor: General ability takes *could*. One successful occasion takes *was able to* or *managed to*. A failure can keep *couldn't*.
body.trap: *Could* is taught as the past of *can*, so it looks like the past of every *can*. It is the past of the general one only.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. *Managed to* is warmer and more spoken; *was able to* fits an essay or a report.

body.text: Asking whether you are allowed

body.caption: All four ask the same thing. They differ in how formal you sound.
rows: Can I take one of these?
Could I take one of these?
May I take one of these?
plain, and works in any tense
Am I allowed to take one?
footnotes: In notices, permission is usually given with *may* or with *be allowed to*.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The road was flooded, but we could reach the ferry in time.
body.right: The road was flooded, but we were able to reach the ferry in time.
body.why_it_happens: *Could* is presented as the past of *can*, so it gets used for every past ability. Used on one occasion it reads as *we would have been able to*, and the reader cannot tell whether you got there.
body.smallest_fix: For one occasion that worked out, write *were able to* or *managed to*.

body.wrong: After the training, staff will can use the new system.
body.right: After the training, staff will be able to use the new system.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence needs a future ability, and English has no future of *can*. Two modals cannot stand together, so the two-word helper takes over.
body.smallest_fix: Write *will be able to*. The same repair works after *might*, *should* and *must*.

body.wrong: The new pump can able to move twice the volume.
body.right: The new pump can move twice the volume.
body.why_it_happens: *Can* and *be able to* mean the same thing, so both get written into one verb group for safety. Only one of the two is needed, and *can* is the shorter.
body.smallest_fix: Delete one of them. Use *can* on its own for the present.

body.heard: *Can* means only ability. If you are asking permission you have to use *may*.
also_known_as: *Can I go?* is wrong; say *May I go?*
body.truth: *Can I…?* is standard English for asking permission and has been for a very long time. *May* is not more correct — it is more formal, and in speech it can sound stiff. Some readers were taught the older rule and still prefer *may* in writing.
body.what_to_do: Ask with *can* or *could* in speech. Use *may* in a formal letter or a written notice, where the extra distance suits the page.

body.mechanism: Arabic often builds ability with a verb meaning *to be able*, followed by a full clause with its own marking.
body.wrong: She can that she finishes the report today.
body.right: She can finish the report today.
body.fix: After a modal, put the base form straight in. No second clause and no joining word.

article_json.one_line: This lets you ask for something, offer something or suggest something at the level of politeness the situation needs.
article_json.short_answer: Ask with *Could you…?* in most situations. Offer with *Shall I…?* Suggest with *Why don't we…?* or *Shall we…?*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I ask somebody for something without sounding rude?

body.text: Politeness in English is mostly distance

English rarely gets politer by adding polite words. It gets politer by stepping back from the other person. *Send me the file* is direct. *Could you send me the file?* asks whether they are able to, which leaves them room to say no.
That is why the past-looking modals do this work. *Could* and *would* put a small distance between you and the request, and distance is what politeness is made of here.

body.caption: The same request, from the kitchen table to a formal letter.

rungs.text: Can you send me the figures?
Could you send me the figures?
Would you mind sending me the figures?
I would be grateful if you could send me the figures.

body.text: How to build a request, an offer and a suggestion

body.caption: Three jobs, three sets of words. Only one takes an *-ing* form.
rows: Would you mind holding the door?
*I would be grateful if you could…*
I would be grateful if you could confirm the date.
Shall I carry that for you?
Would you like a copy of the map?
How about starting at the north end?
footnotes: *Would you mind* is followed by an *-ing* form, never by *to*.
*Yes* to *Would you mind…?* means the person does object. Most people answer *not at all*.

body.lead_in: One request, climbing from direct to formal. Only the opening words change.

items.text: Can you check the meter reading for me?
items.gloss: You are asking a colleague you know well.

items.text: Could you check the meter reading before you lock up?
items.gloss: The same request, and it works with almost anybody.

items.text: Would you mind checking the meter reading before you lock up?
items.gloss: You are asking a favour, and you know it is one.

items.text: I would be grateful if you could confirm the meter reading in writing.
items.gloss: This is a letter to somebody you have never met.

marks.span: would be grateful if you could

body.so_what: Nothing about the meter changed. What changed is how much room the asker leaves the other person to refuse.

body.text: Ask with *Could you…?* unless you know the person well or you are writing a formal letter. It fits almost every situation in between.

body.lead_in: Three offers and a suggestion, each with the words that job takes.

items.text: Shall I ring the depot and ask about the delivery?
items.gloss: You are offering to make the call yourself.

items.text: Would you like me to send the notes across?
items.gloss: You are offering to do it, and checking they want it.

items.text: Shall we start with the section nobody has read?
items.gloss: You are suggesting something the two of you do together.

items.text: How about moving the whole meeting to the morning?
items.gloss: You are putting an idea on the table for the group.

body.so_what: *Shall* survives mainly in these two places: offering to do something, and suggesting something together.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: Would you mind to send me the timetable?
body.right: Would you mind sending me the timetable?
body.why_it_happens: *Would you like to…* takes *to*, and the two openings look alike. *Mind* is one of the verbs that takes an *-ing* form after it.
body.smallest_fix: After *would you mind*, use the *-ing* form: *sending*, *holding*, *waiting*.

body.wrong: I want you to send me the confirmation by Friday.
body.right: I would be grateful if you could send me the confirmation by Friday.
body.why_it_happens: *I want* is honest and clear, and in many languages the equivalent is ordinary politeness. In English it takes all the distance out of the sentence and reads as an order.
body.smallest_fix: In a formal letter, ask with *I would be grateful if you could* or *Could you please*.

body.wrong: Do you can help me with the second form?
body.right: Can you help me with the second form?
body.why_it_happens: Ordinary verbs need *do* in a question, so *do* goes in for safety. A modal makes its own question by moving to the front, and it never takes *do* as well.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *do* and start with the modal: *Can you…?*, *Could you…?*

body.heard: *Can you…?* is rude. You must say *Could you…?*
body.truth: *Can you…?* is ordinary polite English between people who know each other, and it is what most requests in a workplace sound like. *Could you…?* is a little more careful, which is why it is the safer choice with a stranger.
body.what_to_do: Use *Could you…?* when you do not know the person. Use *Can you…?* freely with people you know, and add *please* wherever it fits.

body.mechanism: Hindi carries politeness in the ending of the verb itself, so a direct instruction can already be fully polite.
body.wrong: Please give me the second form.
body.right: Could you give me the second form, please?
body.fix: In English, put the politeness in the question shape as well, not only in *please*.

article_json.also_called: *Will* and *would* for characteristic behaviour, and *won't* for refusal
article_json.one_line: This lets you describe what somebody or something typically does, and what it stubbornly refuses to do.
article_json.short_answer: *Will* says what typically happens now. *Would* says what typically happened then. *Won't* and *wouldn't* mean refuses and refused.

body.text: *Will* is not only about the future
*Our printer will jam if you load more than fifty sheets* is not a prediction about later. It says what the printer does, every time, because that is what it is like.
Move the same sentence back into the past and *will* becomes *would*. Make either of them negative and the meaning changes again: the thing is not failing, it is refusing.
The four jobs in one table

body.caption: Positive means typical. Negative means refuses.

the barrier would stick in wet weather
the barrier won't lift at all

items.text: The old scanner will cut out if you leave it on all afternoon.
items.gloss: That is what it does. It has always done it.

items.text: The old scanner would cut out if you left it on all afternoon.
items.gloss: In those days that was what it did.

items.text: The scanner won't read anything smaller than a postcard.
items.gloss: It refuses. Small items simply do not scan.

items.gloss: On that occasion it refused, and somebody did the work instead.

items.text: My grandmother would repaint the boat every May.

body.so_what: The positives describe a pattern. The negatives describe something digging its heels in.

body.text: Use *will* and *would* for repeated actions that are typical of somebody or something. Use *won't* and *wouldn't* for refusal.

body.lead_in: Three refusals, one from a person, one from a machine and one from a door.

items.text: The site manager won't sign anything without the survey.
items.gloss: He refuses, and he has said so.

items.text: The side door wouldn't shut properly all winter.
items.gloss: All winter the door stayed slightly open however hard you pushed.

items.text: The office computer won't accept the new password.
items.gloss: You have typed it correctly and the machine still says no.

body.so_what: None of these is about the future. Each one is about something that will not do what it is asked.

body.text: Was it a state, a repeated action, or one event?

body.question: Was it something that was true, something repeated, or one event?

options.label: *used to*
options.use_it_when: Anything that was true then and is not true now, including states. This is the safe default.
options.example: There used to be a ferry across the estuary.

options.label: *would*
options.use_it_when: A repeated action, once the past setting has already been established, usually in a story or a memory.
options.example: Every August the whole street would repaint their fences.

options.label: past simple
options.use_it_when: One completed event, or a habit where you are not pointing at the contrast with now.
options.example: We lived above the shop for six years.

a.text: I used to have a motorbike.
a.means: You owned one, and you do not now.

b.text: I used to ride to work.
b.means: Riding to work was your routine then, and it is not now.

a.text: She used to be nervous about presentations.
a.means: Nerves were how she was then, and she has got past it.

b.text: She would rehearse every presentation twice.
b.means: Rehearsing twice was what she did each time.

a.text: We used to walk to the market on Saturdays.
a.means: That was the Saturday routine, and it stopped.

b.text: We walked to the market on Saturday.
b.means: On that one Saturday, you walked.

a.text: The mill would flood twice a winter.
a.means: Two floods a winter was the pattern.

b.text: The mill flooded twice that winter.
b.means: That particular winter there were two floods.

body.deciding_factor: *Used to* works for everything that has stopped. *Would* works only for repeated actions, never for states.
body.trap: *Would* looks like the more advanced word, so it gets used everywhere. Put it on a state and the sentence stops meaning the past at all.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere, and this is a strong Speaking Part 1 and Part 3 move for saying how things have changed.

body.text: *Would* also needs the past already set up around it. Open a story with it and the reader hears a different sentence, because *would* on its own points at something imaginary.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Before the bypass opened, there would be a level crossing here.
body.right: Before the bypass opened, there used to be a level crossing here.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* and *used to* are taught as two ways of saying the same thing, so one gets swapped for the other. *Would* cannot describe a state, and the sentence turns into a guess about something imaginary.
body.smallest_fix: If the verb describes how things were rather than what somebody did, use *used to*.

body.wrong: Would my father drive us to the coast every August.
body.right: Every August my father would drive us to the coast.
body.why_it_happens: *Would* for a past habit needs the past set up first, either by an earlier sentence or by a time expression in this one. Without it, the reader reads *would* as something unreal.
body.smallest_fix: Put the past time expression in front: *every August*, *in those years*, *when we were small*.

body.wrong: In my country, people will usually eat late in the evening.
body.right: In my country, people usually eat late in the evening.
body.why_it_happens: *Will* for typical behaviour is real English, but it carries a note of complaint or resignation. Used for a plain cultural fact it sounds as though you disapprove of it.
body.smallest_fix: For a neutral general fact, use the present simple. Keep *will* for things that annoy you or surprise you.

body.heard: *Would* and *used to* are interchangeable for past habits.
also_known_as: you can always replace *used to* with *would*
body.truth: They swap freely for repeated actions. They do not swap for states. *There used to be a bus stop outside* cannot become *there would be a bus stop outside*, which means something else entirely.
body.what_to_do: Ask whether the verb is something somebody did, or something that simply was. If it simply was, use *used to*.

body.headline: Positive means typical. Negative means refuses. States take *used to*.

articles.title: Putting a modal in front of a longer verb group

article_json.also_called: Modals with the continuous, the perfect, *be* + third form, and in *if*-sentences
article_json.one_line: This lets you be unsure about something that is in progress, already finished, or done to something else.
article_json.short_answer: Keep the base form after the modal, then build normally: *must be working*, *may have finished*, *can be checked*.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I put *must* or *might* in front of a longer verb group?

body.text: A modal can sit in front of any verb group, not only a short one
*The pump is running* becomes *the pump must be running* when you cannot see it and you are working it out from the noise. Nothing about the verb group changed except the word in front of it.
That is the whole article. Build the verb group you would have used, then push it one step to the right and put the modal in the space.
How to build each combination

body.caption: The word straight after the modal is always the base form: *be* or *have*.
rows: she might have been waiting an hour
done to it, now or later
the figures must have been checked
footnotes: There is never a *to* anywhere in these patterns.
The last two put the thing that was done to at the front of the sentence.

body.lead_in: One modal, five verb groups. Watch the word straight after *must*.
body.dimension: the verb group behind the modal

items.text: The heating must run on a timer.
items.gloss: You are confident a timer controls it.

items.text: The heating must be running, because the radiators are warm.
items.gloss: You are confident it is on at this moment.

items.text: The heating must have run all night.
items.gloss: You are confident it stayed on while everybody was asleep.

items.text: The system must be serviced once a year.
items.gloss: A yearly service is a requirement. The rule does not say who does it.

items.text: The system must have been serviced in the spring.
items.gloss: You are confident somebody serviced it in the spring.

body.so_what: *Must* never moved and never changed. Everything that changed happened behind it.

body.text: Put the base form straight after the modal, then build the rest of the verb group as you normally would.

body.lead_in: Four different modals, each in front of a longer verb group.

items.text: The results can be downloaded from the portal after Friday.
items.gloss: From Friday, anybody with the link can get them.

items.text: Two of the readings might have been recorded twice.
items.gloss: Possibly the same reading went in the list twice.

items.text: They could be waiting at the wrong entrance.
items.gloss: The wrong entrance would explain why nobody has appeared.

items.text: The old bridge should have been replaced years ago.
items.gloss: Nobody replaced it, and that was a mistake.

body.so_what: The word straight after each modal is *be* or *have*, in the plain base form, every single time.

body.text: Where the modal goes in an *if*-sentence

body.caption: The result half takes the modal. The *if* half almost never does.
rows: the path would flood every winter
if the drain should block again
footnotes: *If the drain should block* means the same as *if the drain blocks*, with a small note of unlikeliness.

body.lead_in: The same situation, with the modal moving between the two halves.
body.dimension: which half the modal is in

items.text: If the survey is delayed, the work will start in April instead.
items.gloss: A delay pushes the start to April.

items.text: If the survey were delayed, the work might not start until June.
items.gloss: A delay is not expected, and June is what it would cost.

items.text: If the survey should be delayed, please tell the contractors at once.
items.gloss: A delay is unlikely, and here is what to do if it happens.

body.so_what: In all three, the *if* half stays plain or takes *should*. The modal that carries the meaning sits in the other half.

body.text: What goes wrong

body.wrong: The samples must been collected before the frost.
body.right: The samples must have been collected before the frost.
body.why_it_happens: *Been* already sounds like the past, so it feels like enough on its own. It cannot start a verb group. *Have* is the part that moves the whole thing into the past.
body.smallest_fix: Put *have* straight after the modal, and leave *been* where it is.

body.wrong: The figures can checked against last year's return.
body.right: The figures can be checked against last year's return.
body.why_it_happens: The third form on its own looks finished, and in a short sentence it seems to say enough. Without *be*, the verb group has nothing holding it together.
body.smallest_fix: Put *be* between the modal and the third form: *can be checked*.

body.wrong: If the council would publish the figures, the debate would be shorter.
body.right: If the council published the figures, the debate would be shorter.
body.why_it_happens: Both halves are about something imaginary, so *would* looks as though it belongs in both. English marks the *if* half with the verb form alone and keeps *would* for the result.
body.smallest_fix: Take *would* out of the *if* half. One *would* per sentence, in the result.

body.heard: A modal can only be followed by one verb.
also_known_as: after a modal you use the plain verb and nothing else
body.truth: The rule is about the shape, not the length. The word straight after the modal must be a base form, and *be* and *have* are base forms. Once they are in place they carry as much as any other verb group carries.
body.what_to_do: Check only the first word after the modal. If it is a base form, the group is legal however long it gets.

articles.title: Not claiming more than you can defend

article_json.also_called: Softening a claim: modality in academic and cautious writing
article_json.one_line: This lets you make a claim you can stand behind, instead of a big claim the next paragraph has to rescue.
article_json.short_answer: Match the word to your evidence. *Must* claims certainty, *should* claims a position, *may* and *tend to* claim less.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I give an opinion without claiming more than I can prove?

body.text: A big claim is easy to write and hard to defend

*Online study is better for everybody* takes one sentence to write and a whole paragraph to defend, because a single unhappy student proves it wrong. *Online study suits some learners better* costs one word more and is defensible.
The modal is where that work happens. It is the difference between saying a thing is so and saying how sure you are that it is so.
The words that carry the strength of a claim

body.caption: Strongest at the top. Each row commits you to something different.
rows: an absolute claim you now defend
a clear position, and the usual choice
a general pattern with room for exceptions
footnotes: *Appear to* and *seem to* work like *tend to* and sit at the careful level.

body.lead_in: One claim about the same policy, at four strengths. Only the modal changes.

items.text: Congestion charges must be introduced in every large city.
items.gloss: You are saying there is no acceptable alternative anywhere.

items.text: Congestion charges should be introduced in the largest cities.
items.gloss: You are taking a clear position and leaving smaller cities out of it.

items.text: Congestion charges could be trialled in two boroughs first.
items.gloss: You are putting one workable idea on the table.

items.text: Charges of this kind tend to fall hardest on low earners.
items.gloss: That is the usual pattern, and you are not claiming it always happens.

body.so_what: All four are defensible. The first one is only defensible if you can really show that no city can manage without a charge.

body.text: Pick the weakest word that still says what you mean. A claim you can defend is worth more than a claim that sounds strong.

body.lead_in: Each of these takes a claim about everybody and narrows it to something provable.

items.text: Remote work may reduce the number of short car journeys.
items.gloss: A fall in short journeys is one possible effect.

items.text: Younger workers tend to change employer more often.
items.gloss: That is the general pattern, and there are plenty of exceptions.

items.text: The rise appears to have started before the new fares.
items.gloss: From the figures, the rise looks older than the fare change.

items.text: In most cases the cost falls on the tenant rather than the owner.
items.gloss: Usually the tenant pays, and sometimes the owner does.

body.so_what: Each sentence still says something. None of them can be knocked over by a single counter-example.

b.means: Less stress is one possible result, and you are not promising it.

a.text: Students must attend every lecture.
a.means: Attendance is a requirement, and missing one breaks a rule.

b.text: Students should attend every lecture.
b.means: Attending is strongly recommended, and nobody is breaking a rule.

a.text: Older drivers cause more accidents at junctions.
a.means: You are stating it as a fact about older drivers as a group.

b.text: Older drivers tend to have more accidents at junctions.
b.means: That is the pattern in the figures, with many exceptions.

a.text: The new timetable will cut waiting times by half.
a.means: You are promising the cut. If it does not happen, you were wrong.

b.text: The new timetable is likely to cut waiting times.
b.means: A cut is what you expect, and you are not guaranteeing the size of it.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether one counter-example would sink the sentence. If it would, step down one row in the table.
body.trap: A strong word feels like a strong argument, so the biggest claim goes in first. A claim that is too big is the easiest thing in an essay to argue against.
body.register_note: This belongs in writing above all. In Speaking Part 3 the same words work, and *might* and *could* sound more natural there than *may*.

body.text: Vary the strength across a piece of writing. *Should* in every sentence is not a position but a habit, and *must* in every sentence claims an authority no essay has.
What goes wrong

body.wrong: Social media destroys the concentration of every young person.
body.right: Heavy social media use may weaken concentration in some young people.
body.why_it_happens: A flat statement sounds confident, and confidence sounds like a strong argument. It also means one careful reader with one counter-example has finished your paragraph for you.
body.smallest_fix: Add a modal and narrow the group: *may*, *tend to*, *some*, *in most cases*.

body.wrong: It may possibly be the case that fares could perhaps have some effect.
body.right: Fares may have some effect on how often people travel.
body.why_it_happens: One careful word is good, so four look better. Stacked up, they cancel each other out and the sentence stops claiming anything at all.
body.smallest_fix: Keep one softening word per claim. Delete the rest.

body.wrong: Governments must ban private cars from all city centres.
body.right: Governments should restrict private cars in the busiest city centres.
body.why_it_happens: The task asks for a recommendation, and *must* sounds like the most committed way to give one. It states a requirement, so the rest of the essay has to prove that no other policy could work.
body.smallest_fix: Recommend with *should* or *need to*, and narrow the claim while you are there.

body.heard: Words like *may* and *might* make your writing sound unsure, so leave them out and write with confidence.
body.truth: Careful writing is not unsure writing. *May* and *tend to* show that you know how far your evidence goes, which is a mark of control. What does read as weak is stacking three of them into one sentence.
body.what_to_do: Keep the careful words, one per claim. Be strong about the position you are taking and careful about how far you claim it reaches.

body.headline: Pick the weakest word that still says what you mean.
